title: Bladder Irrigation
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Feeding and Elimination Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Purpose of Bladder Irrigation
headings.content:
Bladder irrigation is a specialized nursing procedure involving the flushing of the urinary bladder with a sterile fluid solution. The primary goal is to maintain the patency of an indwelling urinary catheter by washing away blood clots, mucus, or tissue debris that can obstruct urine flow. When drainage stops, urine backs up inside the bladder, causing severe pain, bladder spasms, and potentially leading to infection or surgical site damage.

Beyond clearing blockages, this technique is used to introduce medications directly into the bladder lining to treat local infections or inflammation. In specialized settings, such as following a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), continuous fluid instillation is vital to prevent thick blood clots from forming inside the surgical cavity.

headings.title: Indications and Contraindications
headings.content:
Knowing when to use bladder irrigation and when to avoid it is crucial for patient safety. Indications include gross hematuria with clot formation, post-urological surgery care, and the need for instilling therapeutic bladder instillations. 

Conversely, absolute contraindications include recent trauma to the urinary tract where the urethra or bladder wall integrity is compromised, as fluid pressure can cause extravasation into surrounding pelvic tissues. Nurses must also exercise extreme caution in patients with active urinary tract infections or severe urethral strictures, unless specifically ordered by the attending physician.

headings.title: Open versus Closed Irrigation Systems
headings.content:
Bladder irrigation can be performed using either an open or a closed system, with closed systems strongly preferred in modern clinical practice.

- **Closed System**: Utilizes a triple-lumen catheter where one lumen is for balloon inflation, one for urine drainage, and a third for continuous fluid inflow. The system remains completely sealed from the irrigation bag to the drainage bag, significantly reducing the risk of introducing external bacteria.
- **Open System**: Requires disconnecting the catheter from the drainage tubing to manually instill and withdraw fluid using a syringe. This method breaks a sterile junction, creating a high risk for catheter-associated urinary tract infections, and is reserved for rare, specific intermittent flushing orders.

headings.title: Equipment and Preparation
headings.content:
Thorough preparation prevents infection and ensures the procedure runs smoothly. Before starting, gather the following supplies:
- Sterile bladder irrigation solution (usually normal saline)
- IV pole and irrigation tubing set
- Sterile irrigation tray or syringe (if using an open method)
- Antiseptic wipes
- Clean gloves, personal protective equipment, and a waterproof pad

Explain the procedure to the patient, reassuring them that while they may feel a strong urge to urinate or mild cramping during the flush, it should not be excruciatingly painful. Position the patient comfortably in the supine or semi-Fowler position and ensure adequate privacy.

headings.title: Continuous Bladder Irrigation Procedure
headings.content:
Continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) requires careful management to ensure the fluid balance remains accurate. Hang the sterile irrigation bag on the IV pole and prime the tubing to eliminate all air bubbles. Clean the third lumen port of the triple-lumen catheter with an antiseptic wipe, then connect the primed irrigation tubing securely.

Open the roller clamp to allow the fluid to flow steadily into the bladder at the prescribed rate. Adjust the flow rate based on the color of the urine output: if the drainage is bright red or contains thick clots, speed up the drip rate until the output turns a clear, pale pink. If the output runs clear, slow the rate to maintain patency without overloading the bladder.

headings.title: Intermittent Bladder Irrigation Procedure
headings.content:
Intermittent irrigation involves periodically flushing a standard catheter using an open syringe method or a two-way system. Wash your hands, put on gloves, and place a waterproof barrier under the catheter junction. Disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing, keeping both ends sterile by placing protective caps on them.

Draw up the prescribed amount of sterile saline into a sterile syringe. Gently insert the syringe tip into the catheter opening and slowly instill the fluid into the bladder without using excessive force. Remove the syringe and reconnect the catheter to the drainage tubing, allowing gravity to drain the fluid and any debris into the collection bag. Repeat as ordered.

headings.title: Monitoring, Complications, and Troubleshooting
headings.content:
Diligent monitoring prevents severe complications during bladder irrigation. The most critical calculation is net fluid balance: you must subtract the total amount of irrigation fluid infused from the total output emptied from the drainage bag to determine true urine output.

If the fluid goes in but nothing comes out, troubleshoot immediately. Check the tubing for kinks, reposition the patient, or check for large blood clots occluding the lumen. If gentle manual aspiration fails to clear the blockage, notify the physician right away. Complications such as fluid overload, bladder perforation, and severe infection can arise if a blocked catheter goes unnoticed.

headings.title: Documentation and Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content:
Accurate charting provides a clear record of the patient's response and fluid status. Document the time irrigation started and stopped, the type and total volume of solution used, and the color, consistency, and clarity of the drainage. Record the exact net fluid balance for every shift to ensure the patient is not retaining excess fluid.

Note the patient's subjective tolerance of the procedure, including any complaints of bladder spasms, pain, or discomfort. Report abnormal findings—such as persistent bright red bleeding, lack of drainage output, or signs of systemic infection like fever—to the healthcare provider promptly.
